20607-rembrandt:
Rembrandt introduces the Dutch master's paintings through a set of chosen plates and studies. Rembrandt painted his wife Saskia again and again, and those portraits are spread through the world's great galleries. The book guides readers from the famous canvases to the neglected ones.

One portrait of Saskia, kept at the Brera in Milan, is not so well known as most. On that account it is reproduced here. The commentary follows Rembrandt's light and shadow across portraits, Bible scenes, and self-portraits. It is a doorway book, meant to send readers to the galleries with sharper eyes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armenierstadt:
Armenierstadt, in Hungarian Szamos-Ujvar and Latin Armenopolis, is a city in Transylvania's Szolnok-Doboka county on the upper Szamos, an eastern branch of the Theiss. It is the home of a Uniat Greek diocese, Armenopolis, covering northern Transylvania. That see answers to Fogaras and Alba Julia's archbishop, resident at Blasendorf. The city was established about 1700 by Armenians who had emigrated from Armenia early in the fourteenth century and first settled on the Krim and Moldau banks.

In the seventeenth century they migrated to Transylvania, and after a two-year struggle led by Armenian-Catholic Bishop Auxentius Veerzereskul, they passed from Eutychianism, a teaching on Christ's nature, to Catholicism. Under the bull Ad Apostolicam Sedem of 26 November 1853 the city was made a diocese. Its first bishop Johann Alexi served from 1854 to 1865, followed by Vancsa, Pavel, and Johann Szabo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-have:
Bernhard Havestadt, a German Jesuit missionary in Chile, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cologne in 1714, he died at Münster after 1778. He joined the Jesuits in 1732 and sailed to Chile in 1746, one of 102 German Jesuits who worked the Chilean mission between 1720 and 1767.

Twenty years among the Araucanian Indians, spent mostly in their country, showed remarkable energy. Gifted in languages, knowing nine more or less well, he threw himself into Chilidugu, the Araucanian tongue, which he said towered over other languages as the Andes tower over other mountains. His grammar and dictionary preserve that language for later study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-hoc:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Hochstadt, also Hostaden, Cologne Archbishop and Imperial Elector from 1238 to 1261. Son of Count Lothar and Mathilde of Vianden, he died on 28 September 1261. In 1216 he held Wevelinghoven parish near Düsseldorf as beneficiary. By 1226 he was Cologne cathedral canon, later provost. After Henry of Molenark died on 26 March 1238, the chapter elected him archbishop. Frederick II gave him insignia at Brescia that August, and Ludolf of Münster ordained and consecrated him on 28 October 1239.

Early months found him beside the emperor against Gregory IX, but he soon joined the papal party. Innocent made him legate in Germany on 14 March 1249, after Mainz Archbishop Sifrit's death left it vacant. At the new king's election he sold his vote to Richard of Cornwall, Henry III's brother. Crowning him at Aachen on 17 May 1257 was his last act. He lies in Cologne cathedral, whose cornerstone he laid on 15 August 1248.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Schmidt, a leading modern Gothic architect, built and restored some of the great churches of Austria and Germany. Born at Frickenhofen in 1825, he worked fifteen years on Cologne Cathedral, drawing most of the tower plans. After becoming a Catholic in 1858 he taught at Milan and restored San Ambrogio, then moved to Vienna as academy professor and cathedral architect.

At Vienna he rebuilt the spire of Saint Stephen's and designed the town hall, whose tall central tower rises 328 feet above a broad court. He also raised churches for Saint Lazarus, the White Tanners, and the Brigittines, and restored the cathedral at Fünfkirchen. His motto joined German force with Italian freedom, softening Gothic height with strong horizontal lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilles-marie-:
Gilles-Marie Oppenordt, also called Oppenord, was a celebrated rococo artist born at Paris in 1672, who died there in 1742. Sent to Rome as a boy on a royal pension, he studied for eight years chiefly under Bernini and Borromini. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the French Borromini, a master of the Regency manner of salon and boudoir decoration.

With Robert de Cotte he shaped the rich rocaille border and shell ornament drawn from the Italian grotesque. The high altars of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Saint-Sulpice won him the regent's favor, and he decorated the Palais Royal and the Hôtel du Grand Prieur. In 1721 the continuing work at Saint-Sulpice passed to him. He was also an unusual talent as a draughtsman, and his designs survive in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herman-von-ma:
Herman von Mallinckrodt, a German parliamentarian born at Minden in 1821, was raised Catholic by his mother though his father was Evangelical. He studied law at Berlin and Bonn and rose to government councillor at Düsseldorf. A transfer to Merseburg against his will led to his pensioning in 1872. Elected to the Prussian House in 1852, he helped found the Catholic Fraction defending church rights, later called the Centre, losing his mandate in the 1863 dissolution.

Returning to the Prussian Lower House in 1868, Mallinckrodt led the Centre Party from 1870 until his death, alongside the Reichensperger brothers and, after 1872, Windthorst. Colleagues praised his force, dignity, and prudence, and Falk, his antagonist as minister of worship, called him an honourable Centre member, a man who lived and fought for his convictions. Rising to his height in the Kulturkampf, he spoke last on 19 May 1874, closing with Per crucem ad lucem, and died days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-heinri:
Johann Heinrich Achterfeldt, a German theologian born at Wesel in 1788 and dead at Bonn in 1877, became Bonn theology professor in 1826. In 1832 he founded with Braun a journal for philosophy and Catholic theology whose chief aim was defending Hermes's teaching.

Achterfeldt also put out Hermes's teachings after his death as Christian-Catholic Dogmatics in 1834 to 1836, sparking sharp dispute until Gregory XVI put Hermes on the Index in September 1835. In 1843 Achterfeldt chose a ban over signing Cologne's required faith pledge. Hermesianism faded after 1848, yet he clung to it until restored in 1862 and fully cleared in 1873 after submission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian-va: This 1913 reference article on Van der Sandt — the Jesuit theologian. Gertrude Dana Steele lists his works. Little is known of his career. The seventeenth century was his era. The order prized its learned son. His 1656 works are famed. His 1656 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pauline-malli: Mother Pauline Mallinckrodt founded the Sisters of Christian Charity to teach and nurse the poor. This entry traces her foundation, her exile in the Kulturkampf, and her sanctity. The foundress of Paderborn: her devoted sisters still teach on three continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-joseph-: This biographical entry profiles Peter Joseph Arnoudt, a Belgian Jesuit of the 1800s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its records of English preachers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GinocchioGerald:
Gerald Ginocchio, a Wofford College sociologist, presented a conference paper with Dennis W. MacDonald on August 18, 1995. The paper, given to the Society for the Study of Social Problems in Washington, D.C., studies the Kennedy assassination as a failure of institutions. Its question is what such an event does to a society.

Sociology treats the assassination not as a puzzle of shots but as a stress test of public trust. Ginocchio and MacDonald argue the institutions meant to answer the event failed at the task. The paper preserves the academy taking up the case three decades on.
my-double-life-the-memoirs-of-sarah-bern:
Sarah Bernhardt tells her own life in these memoirs, issued in 1907. Heinemann published them in London, and Appleton in America. Portraits and pictures fill the volume. One shows her as Adrienne Lecouvreur, a famed stage role.

Bernhardt was the most famous actress of her age. Her double life joins the stage self and the private woman. The memoirs trace her rise, her art, and her fame. Ads in this edition praise Bram Stoker's life of Henry Irving too. Readers get a star's own account of the French theatre world she ruled for decades.
rembrandt:
Mortimer Menpes wrote this study of Rembrandt, with an essay on the painter's life and work by C. Lewis Hind. Adam and Charles Black of London published it in 1905. A front picture shows Rembrandt's Portrait of a Slav Prince of 1637, held at the Hermitage in St. Petersburg.

Four chapters are listed in the contents. The first treats the recoverers of Rembrandt, those who won back his fame. Two chapters then take up the appeal of the paintings and of the etchings in turn. A fourth covers epochs in Rembrandt's life, and a fifth chapter begins as the list breaks off. Menpes himself painted and etched, and writes as a working artist.
